breakfast.name: Akamu / Ogi (Fermented Maize Porridge)
ingredients: Dried fermented maize paste (akamu — soaked fermented corn)
instructions: Akamu is made from dried fermented corn — the fermentation is done in advance
Mix akamu paste with cold water to a thin slurry
Pour boiling water over gradually, stirring — it thickens as the heat hits
The consistency should be smooth, slightly gelatinous
Add sugar, evaporated milk
The fermentation gives a pleasant sour note
Akamu is Nigeria's traditional breakfast pap
Eaten by babies, children, and adults — the transition food that adults never leave
Also called 'koko' in the North, 'ogi' by the Yoruba
Akara (bean fritters) are the traditional akamu accompaniment — sold together at street stalls
breakfast.description: Nigeria's fermented corn porridge — naturally sour from fermentation, thinned with boiling water until smooth and gelatinous, sweetened with sugar and evaporated milk. Called ogi (Yoruba), akamu (Igbo), or koko (Hausa). Nigeria's universal breakfast, from babies to adults. Traditionally eaten with akara (black-eyed pea fritters) from street stalls at dawn.

breakfast.name: Akara (Black-Eyed Pea Fritters)
ingredients: Black-eyed peas (peeled — the skins must be removed for the correct texture)
Fresh pepper (tatashe — red bell, or scotch bonnet)
instructions: Soak black-eyed peas and rub the skins off — this is essential, not optional
Blend peeled peas with onion and pepper until smooth and fluffy
The blending incorporates air — the batter should be light
Season with salt
The batter should be fluffy, not dense — test a small amount in hot oil
If it sinks and stays: add more air by whipping the batter
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil — they should float and puff
Fry until golden and crispy
Akara is Nigeria's street breakfast — sold from large pots by akara sellers at dawn
The sellers wake at 3-4am to prepare — akara is bought fresh every morning
Dipped in ogi (fermented porridge) — the classic Nigerian breakfast combination
breakfast.description: Nigeria's dawn street fritter — black-eyed peas peeled (the skin removal is non-negotiable for texture), blended with onion and pepper until airy, fried until golden and crispy. Akara sellers wake at 3-4am to have them ready at sunrise. Dipped in akamu/ogi porridge, this is the most iconic Nigerian street breakfast. The airy puff requires vigorous blending to incorporate air.

breakfast.name: Bread and Egg (Nigerian Egg Sauce)
instructions: Fry blended tomato and onion in oil until the oil separates from the tomato — this is the tomato sauce
Add scotch bonnet for heat
Crack eggs into the tomato sauce, scramble or leave whole
The tomato sauce coats the eggs
Season with salt
Serve with soft white bread
Nigerian egg sauce (tomato-based scrambled eggs) is the everyday family breakfast
The blended tomato sauce base is universal in Nigerian cooking — the same base for stews, soups, and eggs
Every Nigerian family's breakfast formula: egg sauce + bread or yam
The scotch bonnet pepper is the heat — a small amount is authentic
breakfast.description: Nigeria's everyday family breakfast — eggs scrambled into a tomato-onion sauce with scotch bonnet pepper, served with soft white bread. The blended tomato sauce base (the foundation of almost all Nigerian cooking) appears here in its simplest breakfast form. Every Nigerian family has their egg sauce formula: the tomato-egg-pepper ratio is family identity.

breakfast.name: Moi Moi (Steamed Bean Pudding)
ingredients: Onion, scotch bonnet pepper, tatashe (red bell)
Optional fillings: boiled egg, fish, corned beef
instructions: Soak and peel black-eyed peas — the same preparation as akara
Blend with onion, peppers, crayfish until smooth
Add palm oil — the orange-red color comes from the palm oil
Season generously
The batter should be pourable and smooth
Optional: add hard-boiled egg halves, fish, or corned beef inside
Wrap in banana leaves (traditional) or foil or greased containers
Steam 45 minutes
Moi moi should be firm but soft — like a firm steamed custard
The palm oil gives the distinctive orange color and flavor
Moi moi can be eaten at any meal but is popular for breakfast and lunch
breakfast.description: Nigeria's steamed bean pudding — peeled black-eyed peas blended smooth with tomato, onion, and crayfish, enriched with palm oil, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed until firm. The palm oil gives the characteristic orange color. Optional fillings (egg, fish) turn each moi moi into its own surprise package. A breakfast, a lunch side, or a party food.

lunch.name: Jollof Rice
ingredients: Blended tomato-red pepper-scotch bonnet base (the tomato stew)
instructions: Blend tomatoes, red peppers (tatashe), scotch bonnet into a smooth paste
Fry this paste in generous oil until water is driven off — 20-25 minutes — this is the tomato stew
The tomato must be completely fried — raw tomato gives a sour, uncooked taste
Add tomato paste for depth and color
Add stock, bay leaf, thyme, curry powder
Add parboiled rice — it should be mostly submerged
Cover tightly — LOW heat only
The key technique: the rice cooks in the concentrated tomato-stock vapor
No stirring — this creates the bottom crust (party jollof)
The bottom should be slightly burnt — this is the smoked flavor of party jollof
The smoky bottom is called 'the bottom pot' — the most prized part
Party jollof always involves cooking outdoors on a wood fire — the smoke is the difference
The Great Jollof War: Nigeria vs Ghana — Nigerians believe Nigerian jollof is superior
lunch.description: Nigeria's most hotly contested dish — parboiled rice cooked in a deeply fried tomato-pepper base until the bottom develops a deliberate char (the 'bottom pot' — the most prized part). The smoky bottom is the party jollof experience; cooking on a wood fire is traditional. The Great Jollof War (Nigeria vs Ghana vs Senegal) is unresolved and contested.

lunch.name: Egusi Soup
ingredients: Egusi (ground melon seeds — West Africa's most important seed)
Leaf vegetables: bitter leaf, uziza, or spinach
Meat or fish (goat, stockfish, smoked fish)
instructions: Fry blended tomato-pepper in palm oil until the oil floats on top — the Nigerian fried-down tomato technique
Add ground egusi — mix into the fried tomato
The egusi absorbs oil and begins to fry and clump into chunks — this is correct
Add stock or water, crayfish
Add meat and fish
Simmer 20-30 minutes
Add bitter leaf or uziza leaf (gives a slightly bitter edge to the egusi richness)
Season with salt and Maggi
Egusi is the most consumed soup in Nigeria — across Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa communities
The melon seed gives a unique, slightly bitter, rich, nutty quality
No substitute exists for egusi — it's a foundational West African ingredient
lunch.description: Nigeria's most consumed soup — ground melon seeds (egusi) fried in palm oil until they clump into golden chunks, simmered with crayfish, bitter leaf, and meat. Egusi is the foundational West African seed: slightly nutty, slightly bitter, rich. No substitute. Eaten across Nigeria's three major ethnic groups (Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa) with small cultural variations.

lunch.name: Pounded Yam
ingredients: White yam (the starchy West African variety — not sweet potato)
Mortar and pestle (traditional — the right texture requires this)
instructions: Peel and cube white yam
Boil until very soft — completely cooked through
Transfer to a large wooden mortar while hot
Pound with a heavy wooden pestle — this is vigorous, upper-body work
The pounding process develops the texture — it becomes smooth and elastic
As it develops, it pulls away from the sides of the mortar cleanly
Pound until there are no lumps — taste frequently
The correct pounded yam: smooth, elastic, slightly stretchy, no lumps
Add small amounts of water during pounding if too stiff
Pounded yam is the prestige starch in Nigeria — more labor-intensive than fufu
It accompanies egusi soup, banga soup, and other soups
The mortar-and-pestle technique cannot be perfectly replicated by a blender
lunch.description: Nigeria's prestige starch — boiled white yam pounded in a large mortar until smooth, elastic, and stretchy. The pounding develops a specific texture that blenders cannot replicate: the starch molecules align differently under impact. Pounded yam is the high-status accompaniment for egusi soup and other Nigerian soups. The labor of pounding is part of the food's value.

lunch.name: Suya (Spiced Beef Skewer)
ingredients: Beef (sirloin or rump — sliced very thin)
Suya spice mix: ground peanuts, ginger, paprika, cayenne, garlic powder, onion powder, kuli-kuli (groundnut cake)
instructions: Suya spice is the foundation: ground roasted peanuts dominate
Mix all spices into a thick paste with oil
The kuli-kuli (pressed groundnut cake) is the traditional ingredient — it gives texture
Slice beef very thin — almost translucent
Coat each slice generously with suya spice
Thread onto long metal skewers
Grill over charcoal — the spice chars slightly as it cooks
The char gives the smoky flavor
Suya should be slightly charred on the edges, juicy inside
Serve with raw onion rings, tomato, and optional pepper
Suya is sold by the Hausa people across Nigeria — the Hausa are the traditional suya makers
Evening suya sellers are a Nigerian social institution
lunch.description: Nigeria's spiced beef skewer — very thin beef slices coated in a thick paste of ground peanuts, ginger, and cayenne, grilled over charcoal until the edges char. Suya is made traditionally by Hausa people across Nigeria. Evening suya sellers (with their charcoal grills and the smell of spiced charring beef) are one of Nigeria's most beloved street food institutions.

lunch.name: Banga Soup (Palm Nut Soup)
ingredients: Palm nuts (fresh — pound to extract the banga sauce)
Banga spices: oburunbebe stick (ataiko), beletete leaves, obeletientien
instructions: If using fresh palm nuts: boil until soft, pound in mortar, add water and squeeze out the orange-red sauce
The fresh palm nut sauce has a depth canned cream cannot match
Fry onion, add palm nut sauce, add water
Add fish and crayfish
The banga spices are specific to the Niger Delta — ataiko is a local spice
Simmer 30-40 minutes until oil floats on top
Season with salt
Banga soup comes from the Delta State / Urhobo and Ijaw people
It's eaten with starch (cassava starch similar to eba) or rice
The palm nut flavor is rich, orange, slightly bitter
lunch.description: Nigeria's palm nut soup — fresh palm nuts pounded to extract a rich orange sauce, simmered with catfish, stockfish, and Delta-specific spices (ataiko). Banga comes from Delta State's Urhobo and Ijaw communities. The palm nut oil's orange richness and slight bitterness is the defining flavor. Eaten with cassava starch. The Delta's most distinctive dish.

dinner.name: Pepper Soup (Goat or Catfish)
ingredients: Goat meat (bone-in, including offal optional) OR catfish (whole, cleaned)
Pepper soup spice mix: ehuru, uda, uziza seeds, crayfish
instructions: Pepper soup spice is specific — the blend includes ehuru (calabash nutmeg), uda (Negro pepper), uziza seeds
These spices cannot be replaced — they define the dish
Simmer meat or fish with onion, garlic, ginger
Add ground pepper soup spices, scotch bonnet, crayfish
The soup should be clear or lightly colored — NOT a tomato-based soup
Pepper soup is intentionally light and brothy
Season with salt
The heat is from the pepper — it should make you sweat slightly
Pepper soup is Nigeria's medicinal food — served to women after childbirth, to the sick, at parties
It's believed to open the nasal passages, reduce fevers, and cleanse the system
Catfish pepper soup is the most popular version
dinner.description: Nigeria's medicinal clear soup — catfish or goat simmered with unique West African spices (ehuru, uda, uziza seeds) into a light, clear, intensely peppery broth. These spices have no substitute and define the dish. Pepper soup is believed to be curative: served to new mothers, the sick, at 'pepper soup joints' (informal restaurants). The heat should make you sweat — this is correct.

dinner.name: Ofe Onugbu (Bitter Leaf Soup)
ingredients: Bitter leaf (washed repeatedly — the bitterness should be reduced but not eliminated)
instructions: Bitter leaf must be washed many times — squeeze and rinse repeatedly
The bitterness should reduce to a pleasant, gentle bitterness — not unpleasant
Boil meat and stockfish in water
Fry onion in palm oil — add blended pepper and tomato
Add meat and stock
Add crayfish, scotch bonnet
The cocoyam (ofor) is ground and added as a thickener — it's the authentic Igbo method
Add bitter leaf — it wilts almost immediately
Simmer 10-15 minutes — don't overcook the leaf
Ofe onugbu is the Igbo people's most traditional soup
It represents Igbo culinary identity as strongly as egusi
dinner.description: Nigeria's Igbo bitter leaf soup — repeatedly washed bitter leaf retaining a pleasant gentle bitterness, simmered with palm oil, goat meat, and cocoyam thickener. The bitter leaf must be washed until the bitterness is reduced to a pleasant note, not eliminated. Ofe onugbu represents Igbo culinary identity as deeply as egusi represents Nigerian cooking as a whole.

dinner.name: Eba and Okra Soup
ingredients: Garri (dried, grated, fermented cassava — roasted into granules)
instructions: Eba: pour garri into boiling water and stir vigorously
The garri immediately absorbs the water — stir until it forms a stiff dough
It should be smooth and pull away from the sides — the texture firms as it cools
Okra soup: fry onion in palm oil, add pepper, crayfish, stockfish
Add sliced okra (sliced rounds release the mucilage — the 'draw' texture)
The okra should be slightly viscous — 'draw soup' is the Nigerian term
Season with salt
The eba's granular, slightly fermented flavor pairs perfectly with the viscous okra
The combination: eba + draw okra + palm oil + crayfish is one of Nigeria's core flavor combinations
Garri also eaten dry — poured into cold water with sugar and groundnuts
dinner.description: Nigeria's garri and okra combination — eba (stiff cassava dough made from roasted garri granules) paired with draw okra soup (the sliced okra releasing mucilage creating a viscous 'draw' texture). The fermented cassava's slightly sour, grainy flavor against the silky, viscous okra and palm oil is one of Nigeria's most fundamental eating combinations.

dinner.name: Jollof Rice Party Style
ingredients: Same as lunch jollof — scaled up
Firewood or charcoal (for the outdoor cooking)
instructions: Party jollof requires an outdoor fire — gas or electric stove cannot create the same smoky bottom
The wood fire imparts a smokiness that permeates the rice
Scale up the recipe — party jollof is for crowds
The critical bottom pot: the rice on the bottom slightly chars and smokes
This burnt bottom is scraped off and served separately — the most prized portion
'Party jollof tastes different' is a Nigerian conviction that has scientific basis
The Maillard reaction on the bottom + wood smoke flavor cannot be replicated indoors
Party jollof is made by women (traditionally) for weddings, naming ceremonies, birthday parties
The large outdoor pot over firewood is the image of Nigerian celebration cooking
dinner.description: Nigeria's outdoor celebration rice — the same jollof recipe but cooked in an enormous pot over firewood, the wood smoke and the deliberate charred bottom (the most prized portion) creating a flavor impossible to replicate on a stove. 'Party jollof tastes different' is a widespread Nigerian conviction with scientific basis (wood smoke + Maillard reaction on the bottom). Made for weddings and naming ceremonies.

dinner.name: Nkwobi (Palm Oil Spiced Cow Foot)
ingredients: Cow foot (or cow leg — cleaned, cut into pieces)
Palm oil (solid at room temperature — used different from liquid palm oil)
Edible potash (akanwu — for palm oil emulsification)
instructions: Boil cow foot until very soft — this takes 1.5-2 hours
The collagen dissolves and the broth becomes gelatinous
Drain, reserve some broth
Make the palm oil sauce: mix solid palm oil with akanwu (potash)
The potash causes the palm oil to change color and texture — it becomes orange-yellow and emulsified
Add crayfish, onion, scotch bonnet, season
Add cow foot pieces — coat in the sauce
Add ugba (oil bean) and utazi leaf — both add bitterness
Nkwobi is the Igbo party starter — served at the beginning of events
Eaten from a wooden bowl, shared
The utazi leaf's bitterness against the rich palm oil-cow foot is the flavor balance
dinner.description: Nigeria's Igbo party starter — cow foot boiled until the collagen dissolves, coated in a palm oil sauce emulsified with akanwu (potash, which changes the palm oil's color and texture), with bitter ugba seeds and utazi leaves. The potash-palm oil emulsification technique is unique to Nigerian and Cameroonian cooking. Eaten from wooden bowls at the start of celebrations.

snacks.name: Boli (Roasted Plantain)
ingredients: Ripe plantains (yellow with black patches — maximum sweetness)
instructions: Place whole unpeeled plantain directly on charcoal or open flame
Rotate regularly — the skin chars and blackens
The heat transforms the natural sugars — they caramelize inside
Cook 15-20 minutes until completely soft inside
The skin will be entirely blackened
Peel and eat — the inside is golden, sweet, and slightly smoky
Serve with groundnut paste (peanut sauce) — the classic combination
Boli sellers work the streets in southern Nigeria
The roasted plantain smell is one of Nigeria's most recognizable street food signals
The combination of sweet caramelized plantain and savory peanut sauce is addictive
snacks.description: Nigeria's charcoal-roasted plantain — whole ripe plantains placed directly on charcoal until the skin blackens completely and the interior caramelizes into golden sweetness. Served with groundnut (peanut) sauce. Boli sellers work the streets with charcoal pots; the sweet smoky smell is southern Nigeria's most recognizable street food signal.

snacks.name: Chin Chin (Fried Dough Snack)
instructions: Mix flour, sugar, butter, eggs, milk, baking powder, nutmeg into a stiff dough
Roll out thin, cut into small strips or squares
Fry in batches in hot oil — medium heat for even cooking
They should be golden and very crispy
Drain and cool — they crisp more as they cool
Chin chin is Nigeria's most ubiquitous snack
Made at home for Christmas and celebrations — also sold commercially
Stores well for weeks — the crispy texture doesn't diminish
The nutmeg is the Nigerian signature — distinguishes it from other fried dough snacks
Chin chin is shared across West Africa — Ghana, Cameroon, etc.
snacks.description: Nigeria's most ubiquitous homemade snack — stiff dough with nutmeg and butter, cut into small pieces and deep-fried until very crispy. Made in enormous quantities for Christmas and celebrations. Stores for weeks without losing crispiness. Shared across West Africa but the nutmeg is the Nigerian signature. Commercially produced but the homemade version is always better.

snacks.name: Puff Puff (Fried Yeast Balls)
instructions: Mix flour, yeast, sugar, water, salt into a thick batter — thicker than pancake batter
Rise 30-45 minutes — the yeast creates air bubbles
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil — they should float
The air in the batter makes them puff
Rotate as they fry — they turn themselves somewhat
Golden, round, slightly crispy outside — airy inside
Puff puff is Nigeria's most popular street snack
Sold at every market, school gate, and bus stop
The yeast-risen puff is more airy than similar fried doughs
Eaten hot — the interior is airy and soft, the exterior slightly crispy
No dipping sauce needed — they're sweet enough
snacks.description: Nigeria's most popular street snack — yeasted batter that rises into an airy dough, dropped by spoonfuls into hot oil until puffed and golden. The yeast rise creates an airiness that heavier batters lack. Sold at every market, school gate, and bus stop. Eaten hot. Nigeria's version of the universal yeasted fried ball found across West Africa.

snacks.name: Kilishi (Dried Spiced Beef)
ingredients: Ground spices: ginger, garlic, cloves, cinnamon, cayenne
instructions: Kilishi is made by Hausa people in northern Nigeria
Slice beef paper-thin — as thin as possible
Make a paste of groundnut paste with all spices — very thick
Coat each beef slice with the paste
Dry in the sun for 1-2 days — the sun dehydrates the meat
Alternatively: very low oven (60°C) for 6+ hours
The result: dried, spiced beef jerky with a groundnut crust
The groundnut coating prevents the beef from becoming too hard
Kilishi keeps for months without refrigeration
Nigeria's beef jerky — but the groundnut paste coating is unique worldwide
The North-South connection: Hausa kilishi sold throughout Nigeria
snacks.description: Nigeria's Hausa beef jerky — paper-thin beef slices coated in a thick groundnut paste with ginger and spices, sun-dried until preserved. The groundnut coating prevents the beef from hardening like conventional jerky. Kilishi keeps for months without refrigeration, making it the Hausa people's traditional portable food for travel and trade. Sold throughout Nigeria.

desserts.name: Puff Puff with Custard
ingredients: Instant custard powder (Bird's custard is the Nigerian standard)
instructions: Make custard: mix powder with cold milk, add hot water, stir continuously
Nigerian custard is the same Bird's Custard that the British introduced
It has become entirely Nigerian — served at every celebration
Pour warm custard over fresh puff puff
The puff puff soaks up the custard slightly
The sweet, vanilla-custard + fried dough is a Nigerian dessert standard
Served at birthdays, naming ceremonies, and parties
The Bird's Custard powder tin is a Nigerian kitchen icon
The British colonial food introduction that outlasted everything else
desserts.description: Nigeria's party dessert — fresh puff puff with warm Bird's Custard poured over. Bird's Custard (the British colonial introduction) became so embedded in Nigerian food culture that it's now simply 'Nigerian custard.' The combination of fried dough and vanilla custard appears at every celebration. British colonialism in dessert form: the food that stayed.

desserts.name: Baobab Ice Cream (Homemade)
ingredients: Baobab powder (dried baobab fruit pulp — tart, high vitamin C)
instructions: Baobab (the African superfood tree) produces a dry pulp powder with a unique tart, tangy flavor
Mix baobab powder with condensed milk — the tartness is balanced by the milk's sweetness
Add cream, sugar, optional vanilla
Freeze in a shallow container, stirring every hour to prevent large ice crystals
Or use an ice cream maker
The color: baobab gives a pale cream-yellow color
The flavor: tart, fruity, slightly citrus-like — unlike any other flavor
Baobab powder is now exported as a superfood — Nigerians have eaten it for centuries
The baobab tree is sacred in many Nigerian and West African communities
This ice cream is a modern home recipe using a traditional ingredient
desserts.description: Nigeria's modern baobab dessert — the tart, vitamin-C-rich baobab fruit pulp (a West African superfood eaten for centuries before Western 'discovery') churned into ice cream with condensed milk. The unique tart-fruity baobab flavor has no equivalent. The baobab tree is sacred in many Nigerian communities; its fruit powder is now exported globally as a superfood ingredient.

desserts.name: Zobo Jelly (Hibiscus Gelatin)
instructions: Steep zobo flowers in hot water — the liquid turns deep crimson
Add pineapple peel or ginger while steeping for added flavor
Strain, sweeten generously
Dissolve gelatin in a small amount of warm zobo
Combine and pour into molds
Refrigerate until set
Zobo jelly is vivid magenta — the color is striking
The zobo's tartness concentrates as it sets — the jelly is tart and sweet
A modern Nigerian home dessert that combines the traditional zobo drink with gelatin
Popular at children's parties and family celebrations
The intense magenta color with no artificial coloring
desserts.description: Nigeria's zobo gelatin — hibiscus flower tea (zobo) set into a vivid magenta jelly, optionally with pineapple and ginger. The traditional zobo drink (the most popular non-alcoholic drink in Nigeria) transformed into a party dessert. The intense natural magenta color needs no artificial dye. Popular at children's parties for the dramatic color.

drinks.name: Zobo (Hibiscus Drink)
ingredients: Pineapple (fresh or canned — the flesh or the peel)
instructions: Rinse zobo flowers briefly
Boil with pineapple peel/flesh and ginger in water
The liquid turns deep crimson immediately
The pineapple and ginger cut through the tartness and add complexity
Steep 15-20 minutes
Strain out everything
Sweeten generously — zobo should be sweet and tart together
Refrigerate — serve very cold
Zobo is Nigeria's most consumed non-alcoholic drink
The pineapple-ginger addition is the Nigerian version — distinguishes it from West African bissap
Sold in plastic bags and bottles at every market and bus stop
drinks.description: Nigeria's most consumed non-alcoholic drink — hibiscus flowers steeped with fresh pineapple and ginger into a deep crimson, sweet-tart drink served very cold. The pineapple-ginger addition is the Nigerian signature that distinguishes Nigerian zobo from Senegalese bissap. Sold in plastic bags and bottles at every market and bus stop.

drinks.name: Palm Wine (Emu)
ingredients: Fresh palm wine (tapped from oil palm or raffia palm — fresh sap)
instructions: Palm wine is tapped from the cut flower stem of the oil palm or raffia palm
Fresh (morning): sweet, mildly fizzy, very slightly alcoholic
After 12 hours: increasingly fermented, more sour, more alcoholic
After 24 hours: distinctly alcoholic — stronger than beer
Emu is the Yoruba name; mmanya ocha (Igbo); burukutu (more fermented version)
Served at traditional ceremonies, marriages, and funerals
The calabash (dried gourd) is the traditional serving vessel
The first cup is poured on the ground for the ancestors — before the living drink
In Chinua Achebe's 'Things Fall Apart' — palm wine is central to Igbo cultural life
Nigeria has the world's second-largest palm wine industry
The freshness determines everything — morning palm wine is completely different from evening
drinks.description: Nigeria's traditional ceremonial drink — fresh palm wine tapped daily from oil or raffia palms, from sweet-and-fizzy in the morning to increasingly alcoholic and sour by evening. The calabash is the traditional vessel; the first cup is poured for ancestors before the living drink. Central to Nigerian traditional ceremonies. In Chinua Achebe's 'Things Fall Apart,' palm wine is the thread of Igbo social life.

drinks.name: Kunu Zaki (Millet Drink)
instructions: Soak millet 12 hours — it softens
Grind wet with ginger and cloves
Mix with water — the ratio determines thickness
Strain through cloth — the liquid is kunu
Sweeten to taste
Kunu should be cloudy white — not clear
Refrigerate and drink cold
Kunu zaki is a Hausa drink — from northern Nigeria
The spiced, slightly sour millet drink is Nigeria's northern refreshment
The ginger provides warmth and the millet provides body
Also made from guinea corn (sorghum) — same preparation
Sold by women in northern Nigerian markets in calabashes or plastic bags
drinks.description: Nigeria's northern Hausa millet drink — soaked millet ground with ginger and cloves, strained into a cloudy, spiced, slightly sour drink. Kunu zaki is the northern Nigerian refreshment served from calabashes at northern markets. The ginger warmth and the mild millet sourness together is the northern Nigeria flavor. Also made from sorghum.
